title: Want to see your Florida condo's records? What the law lets you see, and how to ask
seoTitle: Florida Condo Records Request: Your Right to See Them
description: Florida condo owners can inspect most association records. What you can see, what is private, the 10-working-day clock and how to ask in writing.
dek: The budget, the contracts, the inspection reports, the minutes: most of what your association keeps belongs to the owners to see. Here is what Florida law opens to you, what stays private, and how to make a request that works.

body.text: A notice arrives about a special assessment. A neighbor says the inspection report is bad. You want to see for yourself. In Florida, you usually can. The association's official records are open to the owners, with a short list of exceptions.

This article explains what Florida's condo law says about records, how to ask for them, and what happens if the association does not answer. It is a guide, not legal advice. For questions about your building, the association attorney, a lawyer of your own, or DBPR's Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes are the people to ask.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Official records: the papers and files the law says the association must keep, listed in section 718.111(12) of the Florida Statutes. Working days: business days, not counting weekends and holidays. Board or its designee: the board, or the person the board names to handle requests, often the community association manager. DBPR: the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, the state agency that oversees condo associations.
What counts as an official record
Section 718.111(12)(a) of the 2026 Florida Statutes lists more than 20 kinds of records. The ones owners ask about most are:

items: The declaration, bylaws, articles of incorporation and current rules, with their amendments.
Minutes of meetings, and recordings of meetings held by video conference.
Accounting records: bank statements, invoices, account statements, audits and reserve studies.
Current insurance policies, management agreements, leases and contracts.
Bids for work, materials, equipment or services.
Ballots, sign-in sheets, proxies and voting records.
Milestone inspection reports and other structural or life-safety inspection reports, plus building permits.
Board members' education certificates.
The current roster of owners and their mailing addresses and unit numbers.

body.text: The law also says how long they are kept. The founding documents, the rules and the minutes must be kept permanently, from the start of the association. Bids must be kept at least one year. Most other records must be kept, in Florida, for at least seven years.
What you cannot see
Some records stay private, even from owners. Under section 718.111(12)(c), these include:

items: Advice from the association's lawyer and the lawyer's work product, including papers for a lawsuit until it ends.
Information gathered to approve a unit's sale, lease or transfer.
Employee personnel records, such as payroll, health and discipline files. Written employment agreements and budget lines showing pay are still open.
Owners' medical records.
Personal identifiers such as Social Security, driver license and credit card numbers, and most private phone numbers and email addresses. Names, unit numbers and mailing addresses are not private.
Passwords and other electronic security measures, and software that changes data. The data itself is still a record.

body.text: How to ask, and the 10-working-day clock

Put your request in writing and send it to the board or the person the board has named for records, often the manager. You do not have to say why you want the records. The law says the association may set reasonable rules about how often, when, where and how records are inspected, but it may not make you state a purpose.

The records must be made available within 10 working days after the board or its designee receives your written request. The association may meet this by letting you look at them in person, by giving you electronic access, or by letting you view them on a screen and print on request. If your association posts records on its website or app, it can point you there.
With your request, the association must give you a checklist showing which records it made available and which it did not. It must keep that checklist for seven years.

Copies can cost money. The association may charge its actual costs for preparing copies. But you may use your own smartphone or other device to photograph or scan the records, and the law says the association may not charge you for that.
If the association does not answer

If records are not made available within 10 working days, the law presumes the failure was willful, unless the association can show otherwise. An owner can recover actual damages, or minimum damages of $50 per calendar day for up to 10 days, starting on the 11th working day after the written request. A person who wins a lawsuit to enforce these rights can recover reasonable attorney fees from whoever knowingly denied access.

The law treats this seriously. A director, board member or community association manager who willfully and knowingly breaks the records-inspection rules commits a second-degree misdemeanor and must be removed from office. Hiding or destroying records to avoid detection or punishment carries heavier penalties.

DBPR's condo division lists owner access to association records as something it can take complaints about. Its FAQ says that when it finds a violation it typically starts by educating the association and requiring corrective action, and it may issue civil penalties for repeat violations. Damages are a matter for the courts, so an owner who wants money should talk to a lawyer.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: Check the association's website or owner portal first. The record may already be posted.
Write a short, dated request. Name the records as plainly as you can, such as "the 2026 milestone inspection report" or "the roof contract signed this year."
Send it to the board or the manager in a way you can prove, and keep a copy.
Count 10 working days. Keep the checklist the association gives you.
Bring a phone to photograph pages instead of paying for copies.
If nothing comes, a polite follow-up letter is a good next step. After that, DBPR's complaint form and a lawyer are the options.

body.text: If you serve on the board:

items: Make sure you know who receives records requests and how they are logged, with the date received.
Ask the association attorney to review your written records rules and your checklist form.
Keep the private categories separate so they can be held back without slowing down the rest.
Post what you can online, so many requests can be answered with a link.
Ask your attorney before saying no to any request.

faq.q: Can I see my condo association's records in Florida?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Section 718.111(12) of the Florida Statutes opens the official records to any owner and anyone the owner authorizes, at reasonable times. A short list of records, such as attorney advice, personnel files and medical records, stays private.

faq.q: How long does a Florida condo association have to give me records?
faq.a: Ten working days after the board or its designee receives your written request. If it misses that, the law presumes the failure was willful, and minimum damages of $50 a day for up to 10 days can start on the 11th working day.

faq.q: Do I have to tell the condo board why I want the records?
faq.a: No. The association can set reasonable rules about when and how records are inspected, but the law says it may not require an owner to state a purpose.

faq.q: Can my condo association charge me for copies of records?
faq.a: It may charge its actual costs for preparing copies. You can use your own phone or scanner to copy the records instead, and the association may not charge you for that.

faq.q: What can I do if my condo board won't give me the records?
faq.a: Send a follow-up in writing and keep copies. DBPR's condo division takes complaints about owner access to records. To recover damages, you would need to go to court, so talk to a lawyer.
